title: Ang 12–13: Sohila
hookLine: the night hymns close the opening; the daily prayers are the Granth's gateway
tomorrow: what if you were handed a palace made of pearls?

lines: A PLAYLIST WITH A MIX PINNED ON TOP.
cards: A playlist sorted neatly by genre, except someone has pinned a handful of mixed songs to the very top. That's the odd thing about the Granth's first pages.
The book is arranged by raga, the musical moods, and the raga order opens with Sri Rag. But Sri Rag doesn't start until ang fourteen. Before it, the headings jump around: Asa, Gujri, Gauri, Dhanasri.
Why would a book ordered by raga open with a mix?

teach.b: Look at what's pinned. The Japji, said in the morning. So Dar and So Purakh, the Rehras, said in the evening.
And on angs twelve and thirteen, the Sohila, said at night before sleep. Each Sohila hymn sits under its own raga heading, and the set closes the opening pages. So the mix isn't a mess.

teach.h: THE DAILY ROUND BEFORE THE RAGAS.
teach.b: It's the daily round: morning, evening and night, placed in front of everything else. Some readers call these pages the Granth's gateway: you pass through the prayers you say every day before the ragas begin.
Something to tell someone tonight: a reader who knows only the daily prayers already knows the Granth's first thirteen pages. And the night prayer has a picture worth carrying to bed.
In one hymn, under Dhanasri, Guru Nanak describes an aarti, the waving of lamps, with no tray at all. In the original: gagan mai thaal rav chand deepak bane.
The sky is the platter, the sun and the moon are the lamps.
The gateway closes on the whole night sky.

how: Sikhs say the Sohila at night before sleep, as the last of the daily prayers; in the Guru Granth Sahib it stands on angs 12 and 13, after the Japji and the Rehras and before Sri Rag begins on ang 14.

games.q: you're making a bookmark guide for a friend new to the Granth. where do you mark 'the ragas begin'?
o: ang 8, where So Dar's raga heading appears.
games.why: angs 1 to 13 hold the daily prayers, each hymn under its own heading. the raga order itself opens with Sri Rag on ang 14.

practice: If it's dark where you are, look out a window at the sky for a while, whatever lights it: a moon, a star, a streetlamp. If it's daytime, rest your eyes on one light near you instead.
Let it be the lamp on the platter, and breathe slowly while you look.
